article_title: Empowering Education Leaders in Edtech Procurement
citation: Van Nostrand, P., Shell, A., & Noakes, S. (2024). Empowering Education Leaders in Edtech Procurement. Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org/
title: Use OBC and product certifications to empower district voice in sourcing the best edtech products
description: The presentation's key takeaways state that "OBC and product certifications can empower you to use your voice to source the best products for your students," that OBC encourages collaboration and communication across all school-community stakeholders, and that creating OBC contracts helps with intentionality in defining learning goals and outcomes. The principle recommends adopting outcome-based contracting and certification requirements as levers for district purchasing power.
requirements: Districts must engage stakeholders across the school community and define learning goals and outcomes when creating OBC contracts
target_learners: K-12 students served by district edtech procurement
target_learning_goals: Sourcing effective edtech aligned to student learning goals
examples: The session's stated objectives include identifying strategies to become critical consumers of edtech and exploring OBC edtech contracts
key_sources: Van Nostrand, P., Shell, A., & Noakes, S. (2024). Empowering Education Leaders in Edtech Procurement. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/47852ca7-537f-4f37-84c2-47c4031ef337

article_title: Do Gains from Generative AI-Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study
citation: Mahir Akgun and Sacip Toker. (2026). Do Gains from Generative AI–Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22328
title: Observed practice effort rubric scored from AI conversation logs
description: Observed practice effort is a behavioral engagement measure derived from students' submitted AI-agent conversation logs collected after each of three scheduled practice sessions. Two raters independently applied a consensus-developed rubric distinguishing substantive engagement (E), surface engagement (SE), compliance-driven submissions (CE), and non-engaged submissions (NE). Each student earned up to three engagement credits converted to a proportional 0.00–1.00 score, with qualitative adjustments within a band, yielding "an ordinal measure of behavioral engagement distinct from self-report or time-on-task."
requirements: Submitted AI-agent conversation logs after each scheduled practice session and two raters reaching agreement through structured discussion prior to scoring
constraints: The article states the measure "reflects behavioral indicators rather than internal motivational states"
target_learners: undergraduate students completing AI-supported practice sessions
target_learning_goals: behavioral engagement during AI-supported retrieval or study practice
examples: Scores took proportional values such as 0.00, 0.33, 0.66, 1.00, with within-band adjustments such as 0.77 or 0.88 where strict proportional scoring did not fully capture engagement patterns
key_sources: Mahir Akgun and Sacip Toker. (2026). Do Gains from Generative AI–Enabled Adaptive Pretesting Persist? Evidence from a Retention Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22328

article_title: Multimodal Examination Answer Data with Expert-Designed Outcome-Based Education Rubrics for Criterion-Level Assessment
citation: Jahangir Alam SM, Md Khalid Syfullaha, Saad Ahmed, Munira Akter Mou, A K Z Rasel Rahman, A.K.M. Masudur Rahman, Mohammed Sowket Ali. (2026). Multimodal examination answer data with expert-designed Outcome-Based Education rubrics for criterion-level assessment. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22346
title: Four-stage dataset preparation workflow: acquisition, merging, standardization and de-identification, and final paired organization
description: A reproducible preparation pattern for consolidating heterogeneous examiner files into an answer-level dataset. Figure 4 summarizes a four-stage process in which raw questions and rubric designs are combined with student contributions, scans and metadata are linked, sources are merged and cleaned, marks are validated, identifiers are randomized, and integrity is checked. The article states the workflow "provides a reproducible pattern for consolidating heterogeneous examiner files, validating scores, randomizing record identifiers, and preserving file-to-record mappings."
requirements: Examiner materials from multiple contributors in non-standardized representations
OBE expert involvement in rubric design
Integrity checks verifying JSON-to-PDF mapping and file existence
constraints: Record-level de-identification does not guarantee removal of text or logos embedded within every scan
target_learners: higher education students whose scripts are prepared for assessment research
examples: The 485 records were assigned a randomly shuffled set of unique integers from 0 to 484, and original filenames were replaced by randomly generated unique PDF filenames
key_sources: Jahangir Alam SM, Md Khalid Syfullaha, Saad Ahmed, Munira Akter Mou, A K Z Rasel Rahman, A.K.M. Masudur Rahman, Mohammed Sowket Ali. (2026). Multimodal examination answer data with expert-designed Outcome-Based Education rubrics for criterion-level assessment. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22346

article_title: The audience effect in adolescence depends on who's looking over your shoulder
citation: Wolf L.K., Bazargani N., Kilford E.J., Dumontheil I., Blakemore S.-J. (2015). The audience effect in adolescence depends on who's looking over your shoulder. Journal of Adolescence, 43, 5–14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.adolescence.2015.05.003
title: Consider who is observing when adolescents perform evaluated classwork, since peer observation can impair performance
description: The article's data suggest that adolescent performance on evaluated cognitive work is sensitive to the identity of the observer: "performance on a relational reasoning task in adolescence is sensitive to the identity of the person observing and evaluating their performance". Since lessons, exams and homework are often carried out in the presence of others who implicitly or explicitly evaluate performance, educators should be aware that observation by a peer may impair adolescent performance relative to observation by a non-peer.
requirements: Assessment or classwork situations in which adolescent performance is observed and evaluated by others.
constraints: The article did not test audience effects in an educational setting; effects were shown for a relational reasoning task in female participants from high-achieving academic backgrounds, and further work is needed on collaborative or competitive classroom contexts.
target_learners: adolescents
target_learning_goals: relational reasoning performance during evaluated classwork, homework and exams
examples: In the experiment, adolescents solved Raven's-matrix-style problems alone, with a friend watching, or with a female experimenter watching, with the observer silently counting wrong responses.
key_sources: Wolf L.K., Bazargani N., Kilford E.J., Dumontheil I., Blakemore S.-J. (2015). The audience effect in adolescence depends on who's looking over your shoulder. Journal of Adolescence, 43, 5–14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.adolescence.2015.05.003

article_title: Formative and stealth assessment
citation: Shute, V. J., & Kim, Y. J. (2013). Formative and stealth assessment. In J.M. Spector et al. (eds.), Handbook of Research on Educational Communications and Technology. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-3185-5_25
title: Oblivion stealth assessment example: inferring creative problem solving from quest actions
description: The chapter illustrates stealth assessment in the commercial game Oblivion, a first-person 3D role-playing game where players complete quests. Creative problem solving—"the process of coming up with novel but efﬁcient solutions to a given problem"—is the target competency. Actions such as swimming, levitating, or freezing the river carry novelty and efficiency indicator values (e.g., freezing the river: n = 0.76, e = 0.80) elicited from two Oblivion experts, ranging from 0 to 1. Actions captured in real time feed a Bayesian network that updates competency estimates, which can drive formative feedback or re-sequencing of quests.
requirements: Indicator values learned from real data or elicited from experts
Bayesian network software to link observed actions to competency variables
constraints: In the illustrated case, problem solving (based on efficiency) was valued more than creativity given how the conditional probability distributions were set up
target_learners: Players of immersive games (illustrated with a commercial role-playing game)
examples: A player levitating over the river produced observed novelty 0.375 ± 0.072 and efficiency 0.875 ± 0.072, and the parent node inferred she was somewhat high on creative problem solving
key_sources: Shute, V. J., & Kim, Y. J. (2013). Formative and stealth assessment. In J.M. Spector et al. (eds.), Handbook of Research on Educational Communications and Technology. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-3185-5_25

article_title: Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents
citation: Ivcevic Zorana; Eggers Catherine. (2021). Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8003666/
title: Observer reports bridge the gap between measured potential and enacted emotion regulation behavior
description: The article proposes that "observer reports of emotion regulation can bridge the gap between potential (measured by ability tests) and enacted behavior". Performance tests measure the capacity to evaluate regulation strategies in hypothetical scenarios but do not capture whether individuals actually generate and use these strategies in daily situations. Observer reports from knowledgeable acquaintances (here, teachers) provide information about enacted emotion regulation in real-world contexts. The article argues behavior indicating successful emotion regulation depends not only on ability but also on non-ability motivational variables such as perceived efficacy and value of regulating emotions.
requirements: Observers must be knowledgeable about the target individual's behavior in relevant contexts
Teachers were asked to base nominations on what they observed in classes rather than general reputation
constraints: The observer measure used here was based on a single nomination question, which the authors identify as a limitation; multi-item measures would be more reliable
target_learners: adolescents in high school
target_learning_goals: enacting effective emotion regulation in real-world academic and social situations
examples: Teachers nominated up to 5 students at the high and low ends of emotion regulation ability from alphabetical class lists, with nominations standardized and summed across teachers
key_sources: Ivcevic Zorana; Eggers Catherine. (2021). Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8003666/

article_title: Observed emotional and behavioral indicators of motivation predict school readiness in Head Start graduates
citation: Berhenke, Amanda; Miller, Alison L.; Brown, Eleanor; Seifer, Ronald; Dickstein, Susan. (2011). Observed Emotional and Behavioral Indicators of Motivation Predict School Readiness in Head Start Graduates. Early childhood research quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2011.04.001
title: Conceptual model of observed motivation indicators: mastery motivation behaviors, strategy use, and emotion expression during challenging tasks
description: The article proposes a conceptual model (Figure 1) in which motivation in young children is assessed observationally through three classes of indicators. As the authors state, "we considered the following as indicators of motivation: mastery motivation behaviors (persistence, pride, and competence), strategy use (help-seeking), and emotion expression (positive affect, interest/arousal, sadness, confusion, anxiety, anger, frustration, hostility, and shame) as observed during a challenging task." The model links these indicators to school readiness outcomes: student-teacher relationship quality, learning-related behaviors, and academic competence. It rests on the definition of motivation as the process whereby goal-directed activity is energized and sustained, and on mastery motivation and expectancy-value theory.
requirements: Requires observation of children during challenging tasks, with videotaped coding of facial, vocal, and behavioral cues
constraints: The authors note they were not able to code other aspects of task-focused problem-solving strategies because videotapes were primarily focused on children's faces
target_learners: young children (preschool and kindergarten age)
children at risk for school failure, e.g., Head Start graduates
target_learning_goals: early motivation and engagement relevant to school readiness
academic competence and learning-related classroom behaviors
examples: The model was instantiated in puzzle and trivia challenge tasks administered to 131 Head Start graduates in kindergarten, with emotions and task behaviors coded from video.
key_sources: Berhenke, Amanda; Miller, Alison L.; Brown, Eleanor; Seifer, Ronald; Dickstein, Susan. (2011). Observed Emotional and Behavioral Indicators of Motivation Predict School Readiness in Head Start Graduates. Early childhood research quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2011.04.001

article_title: What Classroom Observations Reveal About Reading Comprehension Instruction
citation: Dolores Durkin. (1978). What Classroom Observations Reveal About Reading Comprehension Instruction. Technical Report No. 106, Center for the Study of Reading, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.
title: Improving comprehension instruction requires first observing and timing what classrooms currently do
description: The article argues that reform must begin with descriptive data: "it is impossible to improve instruction until what goes on now, and with what frequency, is known." The study therefore observed middle- and upper-grade classrooms specifically to find, describe, and time comprehension instruction, and published its category definitions and directions so other researchers could replicate the observations.
requirements: A workable definition of comprehension instruction that separates it from assessment and from single-word skills
constraints: Observations were limited to times teachers and administrators permitted; the start and end of the school year and holiday-adjacent weeks were excluded
target_learners: elementary school students in middle and upper grades
examples: Three sub-studies observed fourth grades, grades 3-6 across three schools, and individual children, with each classroom visited on three successive days spread across the school year
key_sources: Dolores Durkin. (1978). What Classroom Observations Reveal About Reading Comprehension Instruction. Technical Report No. 106, Center for the Study of Reading, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. https://doi.org/10.1598/rrq.14.4.2

article_title: The multi-layered nature of small-group learning: Productive interactions in object-oriented collaboration
citation: Damşa, C. I. (2014). The multi-layered nature of small-group learning: Productive interactions in object-oriented collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. (2014) 9:247–281. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9193-8
title: Object-oriented collaborative research project pattern with phased knowledge-object development
description: The redesigned Bachelor Thesis course organized small groups to set up, conduct, and report an empirical research study for external clients across four phases — project initiation, research preparation, construction, and delivery — each producing intermediate objects (project plan, research plan, instruments, drafts) culminating in a final research article and presentation slides. Shared knowledge objects were requested as part of the envisioned problem solutions, positioning students as producers of knowledge rather than mere course-takers. Groups were formed around client-proposed topics and scaffolded to organize and manage their own projects.
requirements: External clients presenting authentic problem situations
Teacher facilitation of client dialogue and as-needed supervision sessions
An online environment supporting document exchange and discussion
constraints: Studied in a 20-week final-year undergraduate educational sciences course; findings arise from five case groups
target_learners: final-year undergraduate educational science students
target_learning_goals: integrating and applying scientific research knowledge
collaborative design and reporting of empirical research
examples: Groups developed interview protocols and observation schemes, collected and analyzed data, and presented final reports at a Bachelor Thesis congress day
key_sources: Damşa, C. I. (2014). The multi-layered nature of small-group learning: Productive interactions in object-oriented collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. (2014) 9:247–281. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9193-8

article_title: A report on the use of the Kansas Silent Reading tests with over one hundred thousand children.
citation: Monroe, W. S. (1917). A report on the use of the Kansas Silent Reading Tests with over one hundred thousand children. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Kansas+Silent+Reading+Tests
title: Design reading tests to be objective and quick to administer so teachers will actually use them
description: Monroe argues a test should be objective, allowing a minimum of opinion in marking papers, and should require little time to give. He reports that users "found the tests very easy to administer and requiring only a small amount of time", and that no one reported difficulty using them. He treats this as significant "because teachers can not be expected to use tests which they do not understand or which require an unusual expenditure of time". Objectivity, however, came at the cost of puzzle-like, untypical reading exercises.
requirements: Directions and exercises simple enough that teachers understand them without unusual time expenditure
Scoring with a minimum of marker opinion
constraints: Achieving objectivity forced exercises toward puzzle-like arithmetical items, limiting the significance of the scores
target_learners: elementary and secondary school pupils
examples: The Kansas Silent Reading Tests were administered at scale with no reported administration difficulty
key_sources: Monroe, W. S. (1917). A report on the use of the Kansas Silent Reading Tests with over one hundred thousand children. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Kansas+Silent+Reading+Tests

article_title: A rodent obstacle course procedure controls delivery of enrichment and enhances complex cognitive functions
citation: Gattas, S., Collett, H. A., Huff, A. E., Creighton, S. D., Weber, S. E., Buckhalter, S. S., Manning, S. A., Ryait, H. S., McNaughton, B. L., & Winters, B. D. (2022). A rodent obstacle course procedure controls delivery of enrichment and enhances complex cognition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00134-x
title: Obstacle Course (OC): a controlled-delivery rodent enrichment paradigm with an exercise-matched Control Course
description: The Obstacle Course is an enrichment paradigm delivered outside animal housing that "enables systematic control over animal engagement with enrichment stimuli". Mice run a square track filled with 12 object-based obstacles for 1 h/day, 6 days/week for 9 weeks; two new obstacles are added and three rearrangements made per session, so mice experienced 132 obstacles over the enrichment period. An exercise-matched Control Course (CC) uses 12 fixed hurdles, identical in size and run for a fixed duration, serving "as a control for physical exercise". Beam sensors and an Arduino board track lap times.
requirements: Mice must interact with each obstacle before proceeding through the track, and enrichment level can be matched across animals by fixing duration spent on the course or the number of laps completed
constraints: The authors note the labor-intensive nature of running each animal daily for an hour limited the number of mice per group; the study tested male mice only
target_learners: rodent models (male C57BL/6 mice) in neuroscience research on enrichment and cognition
target_learning_goals: higher-order cognition: categorization, perceptual invariance, cross-modal integration, long-term object and spatial memory, cognitive flexibility
examples: In the reported study, OC, CC, EH and SH groups (n = 10 per group) were compared across six behavioral tasks; OC mice experienced 132 obstacles over 9 weeks while CC mice ran a fixed 12-hurdle course
key_sources: Gattas, S., Collett, H. A., Huff, A. E., Creighton, S. D., Weber, S. E., Buckhalter, S. S., Manning, S. A., Ryait, H. S., McNaughton, B. L., & Winters, B. D. (2022). A rodent obstacle course procedure controls delivery of enrichment and enhances complex cognition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00134-x

article_title: Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory
citation: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7
title: Objects-to-interpret-with: representational devices targeting metacognition of interpretation and representation
description: The article proposes objects-to-interpret-with as a methodological notion for RDS education, inspired by Papert's constructivist objects-to-think-with. They are "representational devices that aid learners in developing heuristic knowledge and understanding contextual knowledge, with a focus on the metacognitive aspects of interpretation and representation." Instances include model cards, datasheets, and nutritional labels, which present information multimodally, support active learning, and develop metacognition while revealing the partiality and latent mechanisms of algorithms and platforms.
requirements: Specifying the intended audience and purpose of interpretability is essential, as is articulating the desired balance between model performance and model interpretability.
constraints: The article focuses the framework on a population whose technical sophistication lies in the middle — students of data science.
target_learners: graduate and advanced undergraduate data science students
target_learning_goals: interpretability of data and machine learning models
examples: The course project has students develop nutritional labels for Automated Decision Systems as an object-to-interpret-with, serving as an end-to-end auditing device for the entire ADS.
key_sources: Lewis Armanda; Stoyanovich Julia. (2021). Teaching Responsible Data Science: Charting New Pedagogical Territory. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00241-7

article_title: Design, development, and evaluation of a virtual reality game-based application to support computational thinking
citation: Friday Joseph Agbo, Solomon Sunday Oyelere, Jarkko Suhonen, Markku Tukiainen. (2023). Design, development, and evaluation of a virtual reality game-based application to support computational thinking. Education Tech Research Dev 71:505–537. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10161-5
title: Objective distance (OD) model for computing learners' CT competency during gameplay
description: The study adapts Chaichumpa and Temdee's (2018) objective distance model to compute learners' CT competency in real time during iThinkSmart gameplay. As the article states, "OD measures the distance between the expected/satisfactory learner's score ( S i) and the current learner's score ( C i ), mainly used to provide personalized support and intelligent feedback to a learner." The formula uses the satisfactory score, current score, and total score for each instance of a learning object. In this study, the total weighted score and satisfactory score were defined in the system while the player's current score was obtained during gameplay, and control-group Kahoot! data were manually computed with the same formula.
requirements: A defined satisfactory score and total weighted score per learning-object instance, plus the player's current score captured during gameplay
constraints: The model was proposed for evaluating students' competency while learning in a smart learning environment to enhance digital literacy, as attributed to Chaichumpa and Temdee (2018) and Temdee (2021)
target_learners: computer science students in higher education
target_learning_goals: measuring computational thinking competency during game-based learning
examples: Experimental-group test scores were assessed and computed using the OD model during gameplay; control-group CSV data from Kahoot! were manually computed with the OD formula
key_sources: Friday Joseph Agbo, Solomon Sunday Oyelere, Jarkko Suhonen, Markku Tukiainen. (2023). Design, development, and evaluation of a virtual reality game-based application to support computational thinking. Education Tech Research Dev 71:505–537. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10161-5

article_title: The impact of the learner role in healthcare simulation-based education on learning outcomes: a systematic review.
citation: Amechghal A, Naciri A, Takhdat K, Loubbairi S, Mellouki A, Lahlou L, Nassik H. (2026). The impact of the learner role in healthcare simulation-based education on learning outcomes: a systematic review. J Educ Eval Health Prof. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2026.23.24
title: Observational experiential learning framework integrating experiential, social, and social cognitive theories to support observer roles in simulation
description: The review describes Johnson's observational experiential learning framework, which "integrates experiential learning, social learning, and social cognitive theories to support the use of the observer role during SBE." It posits that learners "can initially acquire knowledge through either active participation or structured observation and subsequently transform this experience into clinical skills through reflection and conceptualization during debriefing." The framework is offered to bridge the gap left by the field's traditional reliance on Kolb's experiential learning theory and the underexplored Bandura social cognitive theory of vicarious learning.
requirements: Requires structured observation and reflective debriefing through which observed experience is transformed into learning
constraints: Bandura's social cognitive theory underpinning observational and vicarious learning "remains underexplored in the simulation literature" per the review
target_learners: Health professions students and practitioners in simulation-based education
target_learning_goals: Clinical knowledge and skill acquisition through observation and reflection
examples: Three included studies (Johnson 2019; Ham et al. 2024) explicitly cited Johnson's observational experiential learning framework alongside Kolb and Bandura
key_sources: Amechghal A, Naciri A, Takhdat K, Loubbairi S, Mellouki A, Lahlou L, Nassik H. (2026). The impact of the learner role in healthcare simulation-based education on learning outcomes: a systematic review. J Educ Eval Health Prof. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2026.23.24

article_title: Obesity competencies for healthcare professionals: a scoping review.
citation: Verboven Kenneth, Wikström-Grotell Camilla, Lehtinen-Jacks Susanna, Davis Mary E., O'Donoghue Gráinne, Tuominen Pipsa P. A., Agten Anouk, Curran Fiona, Cunningham Caitriona. (2025). Obesity competencies for healthcare professionals: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07973-3
title: Eleven-domain taxonomy of obesity competencies for healthcare professional education
description: A taxonomy organising obesity-related competencies for HCP education into eleven domains: Obesity Background, Clinical Assessment, Clinical Management, Evidence-Based Practice, Communication, Professionalism/ethical standards, Patient Centred Care, Advocacy/influencing Policy, HCP Education, Public Health/Health promotion and Health Systems. Within these, "forty-one subdomains were identified", ranging from pathophysiology and physical assessment to shared decision making and service economics. The review generated the taxonomy through thematic analysis of competencies reported in 22 included papers, and notes the domains "are applicable to multiple chronic diseases, not solely obesity".
requirements: Competency definitions and achievement criteria must be articulated clearly by any framework development team, per the review
constraints: Domains apply to multiple chronic diseases, not solely obesity; some competencies are obesity-specific
Under-representation of some HCP disciplines (e.g. clinical psychologists) may have led to less emphasis on certain competencies
target_learners: Healthcare professional students
Practicing healthcare professionals in continuing professional development
examples: Clinical Management encompasses nine subdomains including clinical reasoning, exercise/physical activity, diet, behaviour change/motivational interviewing, pharmacotherapy, surgery, patient education, managing comorbidities and interprofessional care
key_sources: Verboven Kenneth, Wikström-Grotell Camilla, Lehtinen-Jacks Susanna, Davis Mary E., O'Donoghue Gráinne, Tuominen Pipsa P. A., Agten Anouk, Curran Fiona, Cunningham Caitriona. (2025). Obesity competencies for healthcare professionals: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07973-3

article_title: The frequency of assessment tools in arthroscopic training: a systematic review.
citation: Zhou Haixia, Xian Chengyao, Zhang Kai-Jun, Yang Zhouwen, Li Wei, Tian Jing. (2022). The frequency of assessment tools in arthroscopic training: a systematic review. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2022.2085317
title: Taxonomy of arthroscopic training assessment tools: objective metrics versus subjective scales
description: The review organizes arthroscopic skills assessment tools into two classes. Objective tools "depend on easy-to-measure metrics" such as completion time, instrument path length, hand movement, visual parameters and injuries, often generated by simulator built-in systems or external sensors. Subjective tools are scoring instruments with predetermined criteria — task-specific checklists and global rating scales (GRS) such as ASSET. The review uses this taxonomy to tabulate frequency and testing context across 28 studies and to argue for combined use.
requirements: Subjective scales require predetermined criteria to reduce subjectivity and make evaluation more reliable
GRS evaluation requires experts, with a specific training protocol for evaluators to improve inter-rater reliability
constraints: Motion-analysis parameters derived from simulators or external sensors are limited to simulated environments and not usable with real patients
GRS effectiveness in the clinical environment is not established; few studies evaluated validity and reliability of GRS in actual patients
target_learners: medical students
orthopaedic residents
surgeons
target_learning_goals: arthroscopic technical skills such as diagnostic arthroscopy, triangulation and meniscectomy
examples: The review tabulated 28 studies by objective metric type and subjective tool type across simulator, cadaver, animal model and patient contexts (Tables 2–4).
key_sources: Zhou Haixia, Xian Chengyao, Zhang Kai-Jun, Yang Zhouwen, Li Wei, Tian Jing. (2022). The frequency of assessment tools in arthroscopic training: a systematic review. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2022.2085317

article_title: The Effects of Online Peer Assessment and Family Entrepreneurial Experience on Students' Business Planning Performance
citation: Chun-Yi Lee. (2015). The Effects of Online Peer Assessment and Family Entrepreneurial Experience on Students' Business Planning Performance. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(1). https://www.tojet.net
title: Observational learning and self-regulated learning as the theoretical basis for role-based online peer assessment
description: The article adopts observational learning and self-regulated learning as the theoretical basis for its online peer assessment activities, in which students act as reviewer, author, or both. As reviewers, students "provide suggestions based on evaluation criteria, inspect and learn from others via observational learning, and then make adjustments to their own work"; as authors, they receive peer feedback and revise. Peer feedback is treated as formative scaffolding, and the process is framed as developing self-observation and self-judgment sub-processes that help learners align behavior with performance goals.
requirements: Students must assume reviewer and/or author roles with access to evaluation criteria and peer feedback during the review process
constraints: The framework was applied in a business plan writing course for fourth-year university students over approximately two months
target_learners: fourth-year university students in entrepreneur management elective classes
examples: Students reviewed plans against seven assessment criteria over three rounds in Moodle, with anonymous reviewer-author assignments
key_sources: Chun-Yi Lee. (2015). The Effects of Online Peer Assessment and Family Entrepreneurial Experience on Students' Business Planning Performance. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1057346

article_title: Graspable Multimedia: A Study of the Effect of A Multimedia System Embodied with Physical Artefacts on Working Memory Capacity of Preschoolers
citation: Kien Tsong Chau, Zarina Samsudin, Wan Ahmad Jaafar Wan Yahaya. (2018). Graspable Multimedia: A Study of the Effect of a Multimedia System Embodied with Physical Artefacts on Working Memory Capacity of Preschoolers. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Objects-span tri-tasks test: a researcher-designed working memory measure for preschoolers
description: The "objects-span tri-tasks" test is a paper-based memory test designed by the researchers to measure preschoolers' WMC, defined as "the size of the largest sequence of words correctly spelled in correct sequence able to be recalled by a subject." Words with two missing letters are presented on cards for 30 seconds each and read aloud; subjects reconstruct sequences from answer-option cards, with span increasing level by level until three consecutive incorrect recalls. It adapts backward digit/word span, reading-span and Ospan logic, replacing Ospan's math task with missing-letter recall.
requirements: One-to-one administration by a researcher, about 30 minutes including practice trials; distinct word sets at baseline and post-test
constraints: Paper-based rather than computer-based because young subjects had problems using a computer mouse
target_learners: preschoolers aged five to six
examples: The overall Cronbach's alpha reliability coefficient of the test in Pilot study 2 was 0.72, described as good internal consistency
key_sources: Kien Tsong Chau, Zarina Samsudin, Wan Ahmad Jaafar Wan Yahaya. (2018). Graspable Multimedia: A Study of the Effect of a Multimedia System Embodied with Physical Artefacts on Working Memory Capacity of Preschoolers. article_title: The Effect of Focus Group Discussions on Pre-Service Teachers' Teaching Experiences and Practices: A Mixed Methods Study
citation: Memduhoğlu, H. B., Kotluk, N., & Yayla, A. (2017). The Effect of Focus Group Discussions on Pre-service Teachers' Teaching Experiences and Practices: A Mixed Methods Study. International Journal of Instruction, 10(4), 273-292. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2017.10416a
title: Observe-discuss and practice-discuss: a cyclical observation-diary-feedback-discussion pattern for teaching practice
description: A pattern named by the article's authors in which pre-service teachers observe the practice teacher or a peer teaching, record observations in diaries and semi-structured observation forms, and the instructor reviews these records, groups the problems into categories, searches literature or expert advice for solutions, and returns the problems and proposed solutions to focus group discussions. The article states "The most important aspect of this process is focus group discussions", held every two weeks over the 12-week practice. It was applied with 12 PSTs across two schools.
requirements: PSTs keep diaries and fill semi-structured observation forms during observation and practice weeks
an instructor reviews the diaries and observation forms and organizes problems into categories for discussion
focus group discussions are held with the experimental PSTs to return feedback on the recorded problems
constraints: applied with only 12 PSTs in two schools in one physics teaching program
the control group received teaching practice without focus group discussions, diaries, or observation forms
target_learners: pre-service teachers (senior physics teaching students)
target_learning_goals: teaching competences: lesson planning, student participation, instructional strategies, classroom management
examples: Over weeks 3-10, PSTs observed the practice teacher in weeks 3-4 and 7-8 and practiced courses themselves in weeks 5-6 and 9-10, with four focus group discussions and a general evaluation meeting in week 11.

citation: Ibrahim, H. G. (2017). Utilization of Innovations and Techniques of Educational Technology in Delivering of Educational Practicum and its Impact on Increasing Academic Achievement among Pre-Service Teachers. Journal of Education and Practice, 8(8), 185-194. https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1142431.pdf
title: Author-developed observation card measuring 12 main skills and 53 sub-skills of educational technology utilization
description: The study used an observation card designed by the author to measure skilled performance with regard to innovations and techniques of educational technology in schools where educational practicum is taught. The card "included (12) main skills that were divided into relevant (53) sub-skills." Reliability was calculated through agreement of reviewers using the Cooper Equation, with the highest coefficient of agreement at 89.7, the lowest at 86.46, and the mean at 88.08, which the article cites as proving the instrument's reliability.
requirements: Review by faculty reviewers to validate wording of paragraphs
constraints: Designed specifically for the educational technology division context in the study's setting
target_learners: pre-service teachers (student teachers)
target_learning_goals: performance skills of utilizing technological innovations
examples: The card was drafted in the form of consecutive behavioral skills that can be directly noticed, with attention to simplicity, clarity, short paragraphs, and the present simple tense

article_title: Observing teaching principles in school - Development and Validation of an Observation Protocol (OPTIS).
citation: Mühlberg Theres, Bachner Joachim, Mess Filip, Schmid-Ellinger Jan. (2026). Observing teaching principles in school - Development and Validation of an Observation Protocol (OPTIS). PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0355710
title: Observer training should be completed before using OPTIS to achieve good to very good reliability
description: The article recommends that a three-step, eight-hour observer training programme be realised before using OPTIS. The training comprises individual study of the protocol and user manual, observation of at least one 45-minute video-recorded lesson, and comparison and discussion of ratings with other observers. The article reports that by applying this training, good to very good reliability values could be achieved.
requirements: At least one 45-minute video-recorded lesson must be observed during training, with ratings compared and discussed with other observers
constraints: The article notes that training length itself does not affect rating quality, positioning eight hours midway between common established trainings of 5–24 hours
target_learners: Observer trainees (university students, researchers)
target_learning_goals: Developing consistent understanding of observation categories for reliable classroom observation
examples: During the test phase the training took five hours without video observation and reliability was unsatisfactory; adding video-based training improved reliability in the piloting

article_title: Development and validation of a competency-based evaluation framework for clinical medical trainees in the era of artificial intelligence: a mixed-methods study in China.
citation: Li Feiyan, Zhao Haojing, Huang Qiqiao, Zhang Chunhui, Chen Geyu. (2026). Development and validation of a competency-based evaluation framework for clinical medical trainees in the era of artificial intelligence: a mixed-methods study in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08779-7
title: OBE-based 72-item competency evaluation matrix for clinical medical trainees in the AI era
description: The article develops a hierarchical competency evaluation matrix rooted in outcome-based education (OBE) principles, comprising eight first-level domains, twenty-four second-level subdomains, and seventy-two third-level behaviorally anchored indicators. Each indicator is 'articulated as a behaviorally anchored item, designed to capture observable attributes such as clinical reasoning, ethical conduct, digital adaptability, and teamwork.' The matrix spans history taking, procedural skills, clinical reasoning, humanistic care, AI literacy, and professionalism, and each indicator is appraised across Importance, Feasibility, and Clarity dimensions.
requirements: Items must be behaviorally anchored, operationally worded, and drafted with semantic clarity, cultural appropriateness, and evaluative neutrality
constraints: Developed and validated at a single center (Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University), with content validity primarily reflecting surgery- and imaging-oriented specialties
target_learners: clinical residents in standardized residency training
postgraduate medical students
clinical educators
examples: Table 1 pairs each competency item with a representative behavior, a suggested assessment method (e.g., OSCE, case-based discussion, AI-assisted history module), and a contextual note on how AI supports that assessment
key_sources: Li Feiyan, Zhao Haojing, Huang Qiqiao, Zhang Chunhui, Chen Geyu. (2026). Development and validation of a competency-based evaluation framework for clinical medical trainees in the era of artificial intelligence: a mixed-methods study in China. article_title: Comparison of the observer role vs. active participant role in interprofessional simulation-based education for affective skills: a randomized-controlled trial.
citation: Inam Maha, Tariq Umar, Durrani Rafia, Karim Masood Muhammad, Surani Zainish, Ismail Faisal W. (2025). Comparison of the observer role vs. active participant role in interprofessional simulation-based education for affective skills: a randomized-controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08490-z
title: Use directed observer roles to educate larger cohorts within the same simulation timeframe and resources
description: Because simulation demand outstrips faculty time, expertise and facilities, the article recommends assigning learners directed observer roles instead of requiring every learner to perform. Its trial found observers "educating larger cohorts within the same timeframe and resources, without compromising learning outcomes", with knowledge and self-efficacy gains matching those of active participants. The authors position this as a cost-effective and time-efficient capacity solution for resource-limited and busy centres.
requirements: Directed observer roles with vicarious observation, checklists and engaged debriefing
Simulation design and delivery following standards of best practice, with trained simulation educators and debriefers
constraints: The return on investment can vary from centre to centre depending on faculty contractual obligations, simulation centre rental and availability of trained personnel
Supporting evidence is a small single-centre sample, limiting generalisability
target_learners: Large interprofessional cohorts of healthcare professionals in settings with constrained faculty time or simulation resources
target_learning_goals: Affective skills training such as patient counselling, and team training in interprofessional education
examples: In the trial, the observer group completed the same four-case simulation circuit and debriefings as the control group while performing live counselling at only one scenario each, achieving comparable test and self-efficacy gains

article_title: Integrating Outcome-Based Education (OBE) and Problem-Based Learning (PBL) in psychiatric clinical practice teaching: an empirical study.
citation: Shi Wenjie, Shi Xiangsong, Zhuang Lirong, Zhu Tingting, Li Gongyin, Huang Chengbing. (2025). Integrating Outcome-Based Education (OBE) and Problem-Based Learning (PBL) in psychiatric clinical practice teaching: an empirical study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08212-5
title: OBE-integrated PBL instructional pattern for psychiatric clinical practice teaching
description: A four-component teaching pattern combining OBE goal orientation with PBL small-group case work: teacher-student training, analysis of learning situation with customized goals, group teaching with dynamic adjustment, and a "process-formative-summative" three-dimensional evaluation system. Groups of "4–5 students with similar self-development plans" work with a responsible teacher, and teaching is "optimized... in real time according to students' feedback" via the Rain Classroom platform.
requirements: Instructors and interns receive systematic training in the core connotations of OBE and PBL before implementation
Student career development plans are collected to set customized training objectives
A responsible teacher is assigned to each small group
constraints: Evaluated only in psychiatric clinical practice teaching with 480 credit hours of internship
target_learners: fifth-year undergraduate psychiatry majors in clinical internship
target_learning_goals: career preparation for postgraduate entrance exams or tertiary-hospital employment
examples: The Study Group's teaching integrated OBE with PBL over a standard 480-credit-hour psychiatric rotation, compared against lecture-based instruction in a controlled design
key_sources: Shi Wenjie, Shi Xiangsong, Zhuang Lirong, Zhu Tingting, Li Gongyin, Huang Chengbing. (2025). Integrating Outcome-Based Education (OBE) and Problem-Based Learning (PBL) in psychiatric clinical practice teaching: an empirical study. article_title: Integrating Outcome-Based Education (OBE) and Problem-Based Learning (PBL) in psychiatric clinical practice teaching: an empirical study.
citation: Shi Wenjie, Shi Xiangsong, Zhuang Lirong, Zhu Tingting, Li Gongyin, Huang Chengbing. (2025). Integrating Outcome-Based Education (OBE) and Problem-Based Learning (PBL) in psychiatric clinical practice teaching: an empirical study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08212-5
title: Complementary-advantages account of OBE and PBL integration
description: The article proposes that OBE's "reverse design" supplies clear direction and purpose while PBL's problem-driven approach offers an engaging context for applying knowledge, so the integration addresses each model's weaknesses. OBE's "goal orientation" compensates for ambiguity in learning direction in PBL, while PBL's "dynamic feedback" lets teachers adjust deviations from OBE's preset path, jointly countering passive indoctrination and disconnection from practice.
requirements: Formative feedback channels (e.g., PBL process evaluation) that let teachers detect and correct deviations from preset outcomes
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation; the design compared against lecture only and cannot isolate the specific synergy from small-group, case-based factors
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in clinical practice teaching
target_learning_goals: integration of theoretical knowledge into clinical thinking
examples: The study applied the account by integrating formative and summative evaluations into a multidimensional assessment model covering theoretical knowledge, clinical skills, scientific research thinking, and professional literacy
key_sources: Shi Wenjie, Shi Xiangsong, Zhuang Lirong, Zhu Tingting, Li Gongyin, Huang Chengbing. (2025). Integrating Outcome-Based Education (OBE) and Problem-Based Learning (PBL) in psychiatric clinical practice teaching: an empirical study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08212-5

article_title: SEE+ computerized classroom-based training enhances 7- to 10-year-olds' socio-emotional cognition through observation and inference.
citation: Mayer Sveta, Dumontheil Iroise, Wilkinson Hannah R., Porayska-Pomsta Kaska, Farran Emily K., Tolmie Andrew K., Mareschal Denis, the UnLocke Team. (2025). SEE+ computerized classroom-based training enhances 7- to 10-year-olds' socio-emotional cognition through observation and inference. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0330934
title: Observation-and-inference whole-class SEL activity pattern with four-phase structure
description: The SEE+ activities instantiate a vicarious-learning pattern: children observe animated social interactions rather than enact them, then reflect and infer. Each activity is "structured as four phases with two episodes of observation interleaved with reflective questions and feedback": context plus first animation with questions about what characters are doing; a replay with inference of mental states and emotion-intensity ratings; prediction of how characters will resolve the conflict; and feedback via a resolution animation, guided by a narrator voiceover. Class-level consensus answers and teacher-led discussion elaborate and consolidate learning.
requirements: A classroom computer and projected screen or whiteboard; teacher or teaching assistant leading the activity and eliciting responses
constraints: Each activity lasts 12 minutes and is used as "a springboard for further discussion if desired"
target_learners: 7- to 10-year-old primary school children in whole-class settings
target_learning_goals: Inferring others' emotions, thoughts and intentions from observed social interactions
examples: Thirty social scenarios informed by the English PSHE curriculum and the SCERTS programme were rendered into animations depicting complex social emotions such as intimidation, ostracism, embarrassment, envy, empathy, guilt, shame, and joy
key_sources: Mayer Sveta, Dumontheil Iroise, Wilkinson Hannah R., Porayska-Pomsta Kaska, Farran Emily K., Tolmie Andrew K., Mareschal Denis, the UnLocke Team. (2025). SEE+ computerized classroom-based training enhances 7- to 10-year-olds' socio-emotional cognition through observation and inference. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0330934

article_title: Application of augmented reality technology for obstetrics and gynecology teaching among undergraduates.
citation: Rao Xuan, Wu Qian-Qian, Yang Jin, Li Xiao. (2025). Application of augmented reality technology for obstetrics and gynecology teaching among undergraduates. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07751-1
title: Textbook-affiliated AR software overlaying 3D dynamic anatomical images on 2D textbook figures
description: An AR learning application affiliated with the ninth-edition OBGY textbook, downloadable to mobile devices. The article states that "By scanning the 2D anatomical images in the book using this software, 3D, dynamic and interactive anatomical images of the female reproductive system and delivery process will appear directly on the mobile devices." It supports zooming, rotating and labeling so learners can view anatomical details from multiple angles. In the study it was used for self-guided online learning after traditional classroom teaching.
requirements: A mobile device able to run the AR software and the physical textbook with its 2D anatomical images to scan
constraints: Students reported a complex and time-consuming use process, non-exquisite 3D pictures, and high memory consumption for the AR software download
target_learners: medical undergraduates studying obstetrics and gynecology
target_learning_goals: 3D spatial understanding of female reproductive anatomy
examples: 312 undergraduates studied the anatomy of the female reproductive system and delivery process with the software after traditional classroom teaching
key_sources: Rao Xuan, Wu Qian-Qian, Yang Jin, Li Xiao. (2025). Application of augmented reality technology for obstetrics and gynecology teaching among undergraduates. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07751-1

article_title: Ability grouping in German secondary schools: The effect of non-academic track schools on the development of Math competencies.
citation: Herrmann, S., & Bach, K. M. (2025). Ability grouping in German secondary schools: The effect of non‐academic track schools on the development of Math competencies. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95, 578–602. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12741
title: Use objective measures such as entrance qualification tests or external evaluations to make school placement decisions
description: The article recommends reforming school placement so decisions rest on objective rather than subjective grounds: "Introducing objective measures, such as entrance qualification tests or external evaluations, could enhance the fairness of school placement decisions, particularly for students from lower SES or migrant backgrounds". It targets current practices that rely mainly on subjective teacher assessment and parental choice, which can misallocate able students with long‐term consequences because upward track changes are rare.
requirements: Placement procedures need access to objective instruments, such as entrance qualification tests or external evaluations, to supplement teacher recommendations and parental choice.
constraints: The article directs the recommendation at systems with early between‐school tracking and stresses the "long‐term adverse effects of underestimating (rather than overestimating) students’ abilities", especially for marginalized students.
target_learners: primary school students facing secondary track placement
students from lower SES or migrant backgrounds
examples: The article recommends that borderline students be given the benefit of the doubt and proposes an official protocol for early detection of misattribution within the first six months of tracking.
key_sources: Herrmann, S., & Bach, K. M. (2025). Ability grouping in German secondary schools: The effect of non‐academic track schools on the development of Math competencies. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95, 578–602. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12741

article_title: Perceptions of supervision and feedback in PaedCompenda, the competency-based, post-graduate curriculum in pediatrics (www.paedcompenda.de).
citation: Somm Irene, Hajart Marco, Fehr Folkert, Weiß-Becker Christoph. (2024). Perceptions of supervision and feedback in PaedCompenda, the competency-based, post-graduate curriculum in pediatrics (www.paedcompenda.de). GMS Journal for Medical Education, 41(5). https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2024-41/zma001710.shtml
title: Design observation-based feedback as an assessment for learning rather than an assessment of learning, using open, criteria-guided evaluation forms as a corrective against eminence-based feedback
description: Observation-based feedback works as a teaching method when the educational setting can be experienced as a learning opportunity rather than a performance evaluation: "If feedback from the trainer is informed mainly by an atmosphere of learning and not a performance evaluation, then the desire 'to do it perfectly for the colleague' can fade into the background." The project replaced reductionist scale-based scoring with open, criteria-guided evaluation forms whose criteria span medical, organizational, and communicative expectations, providing a corrective against individual eminence-based feedback.
requirements: Criteria-guided evaluation forms anchored in guidelines, textbooks on primary pediatric care, and analyses of recorded patient consultations
constraints: Effectiveness depends on many overlapping variables in individual cases; highly regimented single-variable interventions are questionable in terms of sustainability
target_learners: physician trainees in post-graduate primary care pediatrics
target_learning_goals: professional communication with patients and parents
examples: The original feedback forms were revised based on the SIWF form, formulating general evaluation criteria encompassing medical, organizational and communicative expectations specific to general ambulatory pediatrics

Perceptions of supervision and feedback in PaedCompenda, the competency-based, post-graduate curriculum in pediatrics (www.paedcompenda.de). article_title: Enhancing cosmetic suturing skill acquisition in surgical residents through spaced learning training: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Yan Xinjian, Abudouresuli Adilijiang, Yuemaier Abudukeremu, Ge Yan, Shang Shiyao, Yang Jue, Zhang Liulu. (2024). Enhancing cosmetic suturing skill acquisition in surgical residents through spaced learning training: a randomized controlled trial. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2024.2363940
title: Objective three-domain scoring scale for cosmetic suturing skills with blinded three-rater video assessment
description: The outcome measure is an objective scoring scale, derived from a quantifiable 5-point design, with "the suture quality score assessed the uniformity of suture spacing, alignment of skin edges, and strength of the suture knots" as its first domain; the second domain rates suture technique (motion smoothness, knot tying, cutting, overall fluidity) and the third rates completing suturing within the specified timeframe. Each participant's recorded operation video was rated item-by-item by three attending-physician-or-higher surgeons blinded to group assignment, and the score was averaged across raters.
requirements: Video recording of each performance with a head-mounted surgical video recorder
Three independent raters blinded to group via unique video identifiers
constraints: The scale was based on Chinese standardized resident assessment criteria and prior published criteria; it evaluates only suturing quality, technique and time, not other surgical domains
target_learners: Surgical residents
target_learning_goals: Objective assessment of cosmetic suturing skill quality, technique and speed
examples: Interrater reliability was ICC 0.990 (95%CI 0.980–0.995) pre-training, 0.990 post-training, and 0.991 (95%CI 0.981–0.996) at follow-up.
key_sources: Yan Xinjian, Abudouresuli Adilijiang, Yuemaier Abudukeremu, Ge Yan, Shang Shiyao, Yang Jue, Zhang Liulu. (2024). article_title: Simulation-based training in ear, nose and throat skills and emergencies.
citation: MK Goutham, Saldanha Marina, Bhat Vadisha S., A Rajeshwary, Vincent Mark Jittu, Ravikumar Aishwarya. (2023). Simulation-based training in ear, nose and throat skills and emergencies. Brazilian Journal of Otorhinolaryngology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjorl.2022.01.001
title: Pair simulation training with objective, standardized assessment to achieve specific learning objectives
description: The article recommends that simulation training be followed by objective, standardized assessment using validated checklists, so that specific learning objectives are achieved and areas for improvement can be identified. The conclusion states that "Objective structured assessment is the key to achieve specific learning objectives in simulation training", and the discussion reports that the outcome-based evaluation method helped objectively validate assessment and identify potential areas for participant improvement.
requirements: Validated checklists and questionnaires aligned with the training objectives
Multiple assessors to minimize researcher bias
Assessment conducted in a simulated environment with standardized scoring
constraints: Assessment timing was limited to the 15-day posting window in this study
target_learners: Medical interns in rotatory postings
target_learning_goals: Psychomotor and cognitive skills in clinical emergency procedures
examples: Day-15 simulation assessment of all three scenarios on mannequins using a checklist, scored under three assessors to standardize scoring

article_title: The application of the spot the difference teaching method in clinical skills training for residents.
citation: Yang Liu, Li Wen, Zou Jian, An Junnan, Zeng Bin, Zheng Yitao, Yang Jiming, Ren Jia. (2022). The application of the spot the difference teaching method in clinical skills training for residents. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03612-3
title: Let novices observe both flawless and flaw demonstrations and then perform corrective actions
description: The article's central design recommendation is that clinical skills training should have novices observe both a standard video and a flawed version containing error-prone difference points, then perform the skill and dictate corrections aloud at each difference point, so that "students can teach themselves by teaching others". Timely correction and feedback after observation is described as an essential step rarely emphasized in prior error-observation studies.
requirements: Flawed videos recorded one-to-one with standard videos by the same performers in the same settings
Instructor feedback at class end for differences not detected or other operating defects
constraints: The article reports SDTM risks student learning burnout and that the traditional method better promoted independent learning capability
target_learners: first-year surgical residents
novices in clinical skills training
examples: Trainees were asked to tell aloud how to operate the modified skill when they got to a difference point during individual performance on a manikin
key_sources: Yang Liu, Li Wen, Zou Jian, An Junnan, Zeng Bin, Zheng Yitao, Yang Jiming, Ren Jia. (2022). The application of the spot the difference teaching method in clinical skills training for residents. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03612-3

article_title: Associations Between Physical Fitness, Objectively Measured Physical Activity and Academic Performance.
citation: Ðurić Saša, Bogataj Špela, Zovko Vinko, Sember Vedrana. (2021). Associations Between Physical Fitness, Objectively Measured Physical Activity and Academic Performance. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2021.778837
title: Use objective measurement (accelerometry) rather than questionnaires when assessing children's physical activity in learning research
description: The article argues that physical activity in Slovenian research had usually been estimated with questionnaires, "which are less reliable than objective methods", and recommends that "an objective measurement of PA should be considered to ensure the accuracy of the results". It demonstrates this by measuring girls with the ActiGraph GT3X accelerometer over five days, applying wear-time and artifact-cleaning rules. The principle applies to any study linking activity patterns to school outcomes.
requirements: Accelerometer data require artifact removal (counts >16,000, constant zero sequences), the 70/80 wear-time rule, and defined wear windows (7:00–21:30)
constraints: Accelerometers cannot detect static exercises and may underestimate total PA; high device costs limited simultaneous measurement, and children knowing they were monitored means habitual PA was not captured
target_learners: primary school students (girls aged 11–12)
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of physical activity as a correlate of academic performance
examples: Participants wore the ActiGraph GT3X for 5 days covering three school days and two weekend days, with counts sampled in 15-s epochs and invalid sequences replaced with missing data
key_sources: Ðurić Saša, Bogataj Špela, Zovko Vinko, Sember Vedrana. (2021). Associations Between Physical Fitness, Objectively Measured Physical Activity and Academic Performance. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2021.778837

article_title: Test- or judgement-based school track recommendations: Equal opportunities for students with different socio-economic backgrounds?
citation: van Leest, A., Hornstra, L., van Tartwijk, J., & van de Pol, J. (2021). Test‐ or judgement‐based school track recommendations: Equal opportunities for students with different socio‐economic backgrounds? The British Journal of Educational Psychology, 91(1), 193–216. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12356
title: For educational equality at the primary–secondary transition, the availability of objective performance information matters more than whether recommendations are test‐based or judgement‐based
description: The article concludes that educational equality at the transition from primary to secondary education depends less on the formal recommendation type than on which performance information teachers can consult. As the authors put it, 'it was not the type of track recommendation that was important for educational equality at the transition from primary to secondary education, but rather which and how much (objective) information was available to the teacher when formulating a recommendation.' In their data, SES played only a minor role under both regimes.
requirements: Teachers must have access to students' objective prior performance information (standardized mathematics, reading comprehension, and where available school leavers' test results) when formulating track recommendations.
constraints: Findings come from a large Dutch city allowing only singular track recommendations, which may limit generalizability to other regions and countries; school leavers' test data were available for only 35.4% of the pre‐reform cohorts.
target_learners: Grade 6 primary school students at the transition to tracked secondary education
target_learning_goals: Fair and equal allocation of students to secondary school tracks regardless of socio‐economic background
examples: Comparing two pre‐reform cohorts (test‐based) with two post‐reform cohorts (judgement‐based) among 8,639 students from 105 Dutch primary schools using two‐level multilevel mediation models.
key_sources: van Leest, A., Hornstra, L., van Tartwijk, J., & van de Pol, J. (2021). Test‐ or judgement‐based school track recommendations: Equal opportunities for students with different socio‐economic backgrounds? The British Journal of Educational Psychology, 91(1), 193–216. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12356

article_title: Personality traits and academic performance: Correcting self-assessed traits with vignettes.
citation: Coenen Johan, Golsteyn Bart H. H., Stolp Tom, Tempelaar Dirk. (2021). Personality traits and academic performance: Correcting self-assessed traits with vignettes. PLoS ONE 16(3): e0248629. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0248629
title: Use anchoring vignettes or more objective personality measures when studying relationships between personality and academic outcomes, because uncorrected subjective measures overestimate predictive power
description: The article recommends that researchers and policy makers not rely on uncorrected self-reported personality when estimating its predictive power for achievement. Its conclusion states that "Using vignettes or more objective personality measures is important to get unbiased estimates of the predictive power of personality for outcomes in life", and that correlations with academic performance will be more useful for policy makers if more objective measures are employed.
requirements: Collection of anchoring-vignette responses alongside self-assessments, or alternative objective trait measures
constraints: Demonstrated in a first-year economics student sample at one Dutch university; the authors call for replication in representative samples
Vignette anchors may themselves be susceptible to structural differences in perception
target_learners: higher-education students
target_learning_goals: unbiased prediction of academic performance from non-cognitive skills
examples: The study compared grade regressions using uncorrected versus vignette-corrected Conscientiousness, Emotional Stability and Risk Preference measures for the same students

article_title: Evolution of an obstetrics and gynecology interprofessional simulation-based education session for medical and nursing students.
citation: Ogunyemi D, Haltigin C, Vallie S, Ferrari TM, Hayashi S. (2020). Evolution of an obstetrics and gynecology interprofessional simulation-based education session for medical and nursing students. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000022562
title: Four-year obstetrics and gynecology interprofessional simulation-based education program for medical and nursing students
description: A longitudinal IPSE program run from 2014 to 2017 through collaboration between a school of medicine and a school of nursing, in which "The program trained 443 medical and 136 NS". By 2017 it comprised five stations, from a "fetal heart rate case-based workshop" to "obstetric procedures including hands-on B-Lynch Suture practice", with OSCE self- and faculty-assessments introduced in the final year.
requirements: Collaboration between the co-directors, nurse clinical skills instructors, MFM fellows, and basic scientists, with faculty including "OBGYN residents and generalists, MFM fellows and faculty, basic science faculty, nursing instructors, OBGYN nurses, a simulation technician, and an intrauterine device clinical specialist"
constraints: The study was conducted at only one institution, so per the authors "results may not be generalizable"
target_learners: second-year medical students
nursing students on their obstetrics rotation
examples: Second-year medical students rotated in groups of 3 to 4 through three stations for 20 minutes each in 2014, using the SimMom simulator for simulated vaginal delivery
In 2017 the FHR module was removed from the simulation and conducted separately as a 60 minute flipped classroom case-based workshop after students struggled with FHR concepts

article_title: Insights into student assessment outcomes in rural clinical campuses.
citation: Shulruf Boaz, Velan Gary, Forster Lesley, O'Sullivan Anthony, Harris Peter, Taylor Silas. (2019). Insights into student assessment outcomes in rural clinical campuses. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1828-z
title: OBM2 borderline-performance moderation method for OSCE and Management Viva examiner marks
description: The OBM2 is an assessment moderation technique introduced to high-stakes OSCE and Management Viva examinations at UNSW; it 'moderates examiner bias around borderline performance'. Under it, 'borderline marks awarded by lenient examiners are more likely to be converted to fail grades, whereas borderline marks awarded by stringent examiners tend to be converted to pass grades'.
requirements: Applied to high-stakes OSCE and Management Viva examinations, where it was "recently introduced to the OSCEs and Management Viva at UNSW"
constraints: "Since this study used only the final OSCE and Management Viva (post OBM2) results, it was impossible to identify to what extent examiners’ bias was eliminated by the OBM2"
target_learners: undergraduate medical students sitting final OSCE and Management Viva examinations
target_learning_goals: defensible, bias-moderated grading of clinical competence
examples: The study used only post-OBM2 final OSCE and Management Viva results, so the technique's effect on examiner bias could not be isolated

article_title: Is an obesity simulation suit in an undergraduate medical communication class a valuable teaching tool? A cross-sectional proof of concept study.
citation: Herrmann-Werner Anne, Loda Teresa, Wiesner Lisa M, Erschens Rebecca Sarah, Junne Florian, Zipfel Stephan. (2019). Is an obesity simulation suit in an undergraduate medical communication class a valuable teaching tool? A cross-sectional proof of concept study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-029738
title: Obesity simulation suit (OSS) mirroring grade 2 obesity
description: An OSS from 'Perspectives Pioneers' (PerspektivenPioniere, Mallersdorf-Pfaffenberg, Bavaria, Germany) mirroring grade 2 obesity (BMI 35–39.9 kg/m²), worn by a standardised patient portraying a patient with type 2 diabetes in an undergraduate communication course. "The suit consists of two parts: the soft outer shell imitating the typical figure of a patient with obesity, and a series of weights worn inside to simulate the additional weight." It was evaluated for simulated authenticity, didactic profit and physical strain by students, teachers and SPs.
requirements: Worn by a trained standardised patient from the faculty's SP programme within a communication course session
A considerate choice of clothing style for the SP wearing the OSS to guarantee a realistic scenario
constraints: The study was conducted only in a simulated environment and not with real patients with obesity
Only female SPs were used, so gender-specific differences could not be taken into account
target_learners: second-year undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: doctor-patient communication with patients with obesity
examples: In the teaching session, the SP presented as a patient with type 2 diabetes struggling with self-care at a routine GP follow-up; students in small groups of 10 took histories and explored psychosocial factors.
key_sources: Herrmann-Werner Anne, Loda Teresa, Wiesner Lisa M, Erschens Rebecca Sarah, Junne Florian, Zipfel Stephan. (2019). Is an obesity simulation suit in an undergraduate medical communication class a valuable teaching tool? A cross-sectional proof of concept study.
